title: Self-harm: NICE NG225 assessment and care
blurb: Give compassionate, timely care after self-harm: psychosocial assessment without delay, aftercare in 48 hours, the right therapies and safe harm minimisation.
question: Ms Jones, 24, attends the emergency department after cutting her forearm. She has drunk alcohol, and the triage nurse suggests waiting until she is sober and her wounds are sutured before the mental health liaison team sees her. What does NICE NG225 advise?

teach.body: NICE NG225 uses self-harm to mean any act of self-poisoning or self-injury, irrespective of motivation or apparent purpose. It includes acts with and without suicidal intent; non-suicidal self-injury still carries a raised risk of suicide. In plain English: whatever the reason, hurting yourself on purpose is self-harm, deserves the same respect and care, and each episode is understood in its own right.

steps.label: Psychosocial assessment
steps.sub: At the earliest opportunity, alongside physical care (1.5.1-1.5.2, 1.7.3)

steps.label: Care plan and safety plan
steps.sub: Written with the person; copy given (1.5.15-1.5.16)

steps.label: Initial aftercare
steps.sub: Within 48 hours if ongoing safety concerns (1.10.2)

steps.label: Interventions
steps.sub: CBT-informed therapy; DBT-A for some young people (1.11.3-1.11.4)

teach.h: Scenario: Ms Jones in the emergency department
teach.body: NG225 is clear: the psychosocial assessment is not delayed until wounds are sutured or because of her breath alcohol. Staff Nurse Mensah agrees immediate help with Ms Jones and the liaison nurse, cleans and dresses the wounds, and moves her to the private assessment room. When Ms Jones asks for a female clinician, this is arranged. The liaison nurse explores what the cutting does for her, her strengths and needs, and they write a care plan and safety plan together, with aftercare in 48 hours.

teach.text: Attitudes are care too. Phrases like 'attention-seeking' or 'just a cutter', delaying treatment, or refusing local anaesthetic for suturing are punitive. NG225 asks for compassion, non-judgemental language and training that explores staff attitudes and stigma (1.7.5, 1.14.1-1.14.2).

items: Consider the toxicity of medicines in overdose (for example opioids, tricyclics).
Use shared decisions about smaller supplies, such as weekly prescriptions.
Ask the person to return unwanted medicines.
Consider a medicines review after an episode.
Self-harm = any self-poisoning or self-injury, whatever the motive.
Psychosocial assessment at the earliest opportunity, alongside physical care, not delayed by alcohol levels.
Care plan and safety plan written with the person; aftercare within 48 hours if ongoing concerns.
Adults: CBT-informed therapy (4-10 sessions); young people: consider DBT-A. No drugs to reduce self-harm.
Harm minimisation only within ongoing, agreed care; trained staff for observation; no punitive responses.

summary: You can now apply NICE NG225 to people who self-harm: timely psychosocial assessment, collaborative care and safety planning, 48-hour aftercare and the recommended therapies. You can also explain the limits of harm minimisation and challenge punitive attitudes and practices.

A.q: Under NICE NG225, within what time should initial aftercare be provided if there are ongoing safety concerns after a psychosocial assessment?
options: Within 24 hours
Within 48 hours
Within 72 hours
Within 7 days
A.why: NG225 1.10.2: if there are ongoing safety concerns, provide initial aftercare within 48 hours of the psychosocial assessment.

whyNot.0: 24 hours is not the NG225 aftercare timeframe.
whyNot.2: 72 hours is longer than the NG225 timeframe.
whyNot.3: Seven days is the NG53 post-discharge standard, not NG225 aftercare.

A.q: Which psychological intervention does NICE NG225 recommend offering adults who self-harm?
options: Structured CBT-informed therapy for self-harm
Psychodynamic therapy for at least 2 years
A single session of psychoeducation
Group mindfulness without individual work
A.why: NG225 1.11.3: offer a structured, person-centred, CBT-informed psychological intervention specifically tailored for adults who self-harm, typically 4-10 sessions.

whyNot.1: Long-term psychodynamic therapy is not the NG225 recommendation.
whyNot.2: A single session is not the structured intervention NG225 describes.
whyNot.3: Group mindfulness alone is not the recommended intervention.

A.q: What does NICE NG225 say about drug treatment for reducing self-harm?
options: Offer an SSRI to all adults who self-harm
Offer an antipsychotic for repeated self-harm
Offer mood stabilisers if self-harm is frequent
Do not offer drugs specifically to reduce it
A.why: NG225 1.11.10: do not offer drug treatment as a specific intervention to reduce self-harm. Coexisting conditions are treated in their own right.

whyNot.0: SSRIs may treat coexisting depression but are not offered to reduce self-harm itself.
whyNot.1: Antipsychotics are not recommended to reduce self-harm.
whyNot.2: Mood stabilisers are not recommended to reduce self-harm.

B.q: Ms Dale, 28, has attended the emergency department 12 times in three months after self-harm. A colleague suggests a community protection notice. What does NICE NG225 recommend?
options: Issue the notice to reduce attendances
Ask the police to warn her about attending
Hold a multidisciplinary review with her
Refuse treatment unless she engages
B.why: NG225 1.5.17 and 1.7.5: arrange a multidisciplinary review with the person for frequent self-harm and do not use punitive or criminal justice approaches.

whyNot.0: Community protection notices are named in NG225 1.7.5 as approaches not to use.
whyNot.1: Police warnings are a criminal justice response NG225 rules out.
whyNot.3: Conditional treatment is punitive and unsafe.

B.q: Leah, 15, self-harms several times a week and has significant emotional dysregulation. Which intervention should be considered under NICE NG225?
options: Fluoxetine to reduce the self-harm
DBT adapted for adolescents (DBT-A)
A brief 2-session problem-solving course
Admission until the urges have stopped
B.why: NG225 1.11.4: for children and young people with significant emotional dysregulation and frequent self-harm, consider DBT-A.

whyNot.0: Drugs are not offered to reduce self-harm (1.11.10).
whyNot.2: A brief course is not the recommended intervention here.
whyNot.3: Admission is not a treatment for self-harm itself and may not be least restrictive.

B.q: Ms Hill, 19, is on a general medical ward after an overdose, and the teams agree she needs close observation. Who should carry it out according to NICE NG225?
options: A hospital security officer at the bay entrance
A healthcare student on her first placement
A healthcare assistant from another ward
Staff trained in clinical observation
B.why: NG225 1.12.2 and 1.7.23: do not use staff untrained in clinical observation (such as security staff or trainees); observation is by appropriately skilled staff and reviewed regularly.

whyNot.0: Security staff are named as untrained in clinical observation.
whyNot.1: Trainee staff are named as unsuitable for this role.
whyNot.2: Which ward they come from is not the criterion; training in clinical observation is.

C.q: Mr Ross, 26, an in-patient engaged in recovery-focused care, cannot yet resist the urge to cut and asks how to look after his wounds. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Refuse, as discussing it may encourage self-harm
Give him sterile blades to reduce infection
Discuss wound care and delaying, agreed with the team
Remove all his belongings and start continuous observation
C.why: NG225 1.11.11-1.11.12: for someone in ongoing care who cannot yet resist, consider harm minimisation such as wound hygiene, aftercare, distraction and delaying, agreed collaboratively with the MDT.

whyNot.0: Refusing to discuss wound care leaves him at risk of complications.
whyNot.1: NG225 makes no recommendation on 'safer self-harm' such as supplying implements.
whyNot.3: Blanket removal and continuous observation are not the first response to a request for wound care.

C.q: Ms Lowe, 30, attends the emergency department after an overdose. Before her psychosocial assessment, she says she is leaving. What should the nurse do first?
options: Let her go and send a letter to her GP
Assess her safety and mental health before she leaves
Hold her using mechanical restraint until assessed
Tell her she cannot leave until she is assessed
C.why: NG225 1.5.14: if a person wants to leave before a full psychosocial assessment, assess their safety and any mental health problems before they leave; 1.7.18 rules out mechanical restraint in ED.

whyNot.0: Letting her go without any assessment ignores immediate risk after an overdose.
whyNot.2: NG225 1.7.18: do not use mechanical restraint in ED to prevent a person leaving.
whyNot.3: Detaining her requires a lawful basis; the first step is assessing safety and capacity.

C.q: Ms Grey, 45, has twice overdosed on her prescribed antidepressant. She is engaged with her community team. Which prescribing approach best follows NICE NG225?
options: Stop the antidepressant without review
Prescribe 3 months' supply to reduce visits
Switch to a tricyclic, which is better tolerated
Agree smaller weekly supplies with her
C.why: NG225 1.13.2: use shared decision-making to discuss limiting the quantity supplied (for example weekly prescriptions) and ask for unwanted medicines to be returned.

whyNot.0: Stopping abruptly risks withdrawal and relapse, and is not shared decision-making.
whyNot.1: Larger supplies increase the amount available for overdose.
whyNot.2: Tricyclics are more toxic in overdose (1.13.1).

reteach.title: Timely, private, collaborative
reteach.question: What are the non-negotiables in self-harm care?

blocks.body: Timely: psychosocial assessment at the earliest opportunity, alongside physical care, not after it, and not delayed by alcohol. Private: a designated room, with a same-sex assessor if asked. Collaborative: a care plan and safety plan written with the person, aftercare within 48 hours if concerns continue, and no punitive responses.

blocks.text: Being intoxicated or still needing sutures is not a reason to delay the psychosocial assessment.

explain.body: A mental health professional carries out a psychosocial assessment at the earliest opportunity after self-harm. Do not delay it until medical treatment is complete or because of breath or blood alcohol levels.

test.q: A man who has self-harmed has been drinking. When should his psychosocial assessment happen under NICE NG225?
options: When his breath alcohol reaches zero
At the earliest opportunity, with support
The day after he is medically fit
At his next GP appointment
test.why: NG225 1.5.1-1.5.4: assess at the earliest opportunity; agree immediate help if intoxicated and do not use alcohol levels to delay assessment.

whyNot.0: Alcohol levels must not be used to delay the assessment.
whyNot.2: Do not delay until medical treatment is completed.
whyNot.3: Deferring to primary care delays assessment and care.

explain.body: Assess in a private, designated area where the person cannot be overheard. Offer a same-sex professional if requested, and adapt for learning disability, autism or other conditions. Explore the functions of self-harm; each episode is understood in its own right.

test.q: Where should a psychosocial assessment after self-harm take place?
options: In a private area where they cannot be overheard
In the waiting room to keep them near staff
In a curtained cubicle in the main department
In the corridor, so they can be seen quickly
test.why: NG225 1.5.7 and 1.7.15: carry out the assessment in a private, designated area where it is possible to speak in confidence without being overheard.

whyNot.1: A waiting room is public and not private.
whyNot.2: Curtains do not stop conversations being overheard.

explain.body: Adults: a structured, CBT-informed intervention tailored to self-harm, typically 4-10 sessions. Young people with frequent self-harm and significant emotional dysregulation: consider DBT-A. No drugs as a specific treatment for self-harm.

test.q: How many sessions does a CBT-informed self-harm intervention for adults typically involve under NICE NG225?
options: 1 to 2
4 to 10
test.why: NG225 1.11.3: typically between 4 and 10 sessions, with more if needed.

whyNot.0: One or two sessions is below the typical NG225 range.
whyNot.3: 26-40 sessions is far above the NG225 range.

explain.body: Harm minimisation is considered only for someone in ongoing care who cannot yet resist, agreed with them and the MDT: wound hygiene, delaying, coping and facts about risks. Punitive, aversive or criminal justice responses are not used.

test.q: Which is an example of a harm minimisation strategy that NICE NG225 suggests discussing?
options: Wound hygiene and aftercare
Supplying clean blades for cutting
Agreeing a weekly limit on cuts
Prosecution for repeated attendances
test.why: NG225 1.11.12 lists wound hygiene and aftercare, distraction, self-care, information about complications and the effect of alcohol and drugs on urges.

whyNot.1: NG225 makes no recommendation on 'safer self-harm' such as supplying implements.
whyNot.2: Agreeing a quota is not an NG225 strategy.
whyNot.3: Criminal justice approaches are ruled out (1.7.5).
